title: A keyboard for XR that reads the hands
subtitle: Typing in a headset with nothing under the fingers
role: Concept, interaction and interface design, and the working prototype of the recognition logic
summary: This is a 2024 concept and working prototype for typing inside an XR headset without a physical keyboard and without pointing at floating keys. A camera watches both hands, treats each finger as a small group of letters, and surfaces the matching words above the hands. I designed the interaction and built the working recognition logic.

sections.heading: Keeping the typing habit
sections.body:
Text entry in headsets still feels awkward. A physical keyboard anchors a person to a desk. A floating keyboard turns typing into aiming at one key at a time and looking down to hit each target.

People already know how to type; their fingers know where to go before the eyes check. The starting idea was to keep that finger habit intact and take the physical board away.

sections.heading: Eight fingers, one word list
sections.body:
The prototype watches both hands through a camera and tracks 21 landmarks on each hand. Whenever a fingertip dips, the system registers a press. Eight fingers carry the alphabet, excluding the thumbs, with three or four letters assigned to each finger.

A single finger dip is ambiguous because it could mean a, b or c. A sequence of dips narrows rapidly. The prototype scans a list of common words and keeps every word whose letters fall inside those finger groups in that order, trimming the list with every press.

The panel below runs the same recognition logic inside this page. Click a finger to bend it, or press 1 to 8 on the keyboard.

sections.heading: Picking the matching word
sections.body: Some sequences still match more than one word. Home, good and gone share the exact same four fingers. To settle those collisions without breaking flow, the matching candidates appear in a quiet row floating above the hands, and a pinch confirms the highlighted word. Keeping the row directly in front of the hands lets the eyes stay up.

sections.heading: Adapting to each typist
sections.body:
No two people distribute keys across their fingers in quite the same way. In the full interaction flow, first-time setup asks the wearer to type a sentence on any physical keyboard while the headset watches their hands, learning which finger hits which letters so the eight groups follow their own habit. In the current prototype, those groups stay fixed in alphabetical order.

Right now, the recognition logic runs as a desktop prototype using a laptop camera and open-source hand tracking. The headset views are Figma frames laid over press photographs of a headset in use.
